klein.label: Kleinprofil, the narrow trains
klein.widthText: About 2.30 m on the classic design, about 2.40 m on newer trains

lines.note: The oldest stretch in the city and the quietest of the narrow lines in 2024, at about 55,900 riders a weekday. Expect a narrow car, a short train and a lot of viaduct east of Gleisdreieck.

lines.trains: New JK trains since 8 September 2025, plus older cars
lines.note: The new JK trains started here. It is also the slowest line on average, 25.6 km/h in 2024, because the stations sit close together on the old route. Narrow cars fill fast at Alexanderplatz and Potsdamer Platz.

lines.trains: IK18 trains and older cars moved over from the U2
lines.note: A narrow line through the south-west with about 165,300 riders a weekday in 2024. Since the December 2025 timetable trains run with up to eight cars.

lines.opened: 1910, built by the town of Schöneberg
lines.note: The shortest line, with about 14,200 riders a weekday in 2024. It opened in 1910 as the first municipal U-Bahn in Germany. If a narrow car feels empty anywhere, it is here.

lines.trains: New J trains since 18 May 2026, plus IK cars with gap boards
lines.note: A wide line that still runs some narrow-based IK cars. They carry bolted-on boards along the lower body to close the gap to the wide platforms, so watch the step on those. The new J trains took over regular service here first.
The first line built wide, opened on 30 January 1923. About 324,000 riders a weekday in 2024. The wider car means more room in the doorways at Friedrichstraße and Hallesches Tor.
The longest and busiest line: about 463,100 riders a weekday in 2024, and the fastest on average at 32.9 km/h. Wide cars, long trains, long distances.
About 331,400 riders a weekday in 2024, the second busiest. Wide cars through Kottbusser Tor, Hermannplatz and Alexanderplatz.

lines.trains: New J trains since October 2026, plus older wide trains
lines.note: The youngest of these lines, opened in 1961 in West Berlin. About 258,400 riders a weekday in 2024, and since October 2026 you can catch one of the new J trains here.

foot: Car widths and heights from BVG and published train data; rider numbers are 2024 weekday averages from the Berlin Senate's answer 19/24551. The tunnel opening is drawn as a schematic, not to a survey.
